Deborah Pereg

Information Theoretic Perspective on Representation Learning

Deborah Pereg deborah.pereg@supsi.ch Affiliation: Istituto Dalle Molle di Studi sull’Intelligenza Artificiale (IDSIA), Affiliation: Scuola Universitaria Professionale della Svizzera Italiana (SUPSI), Affiliation: Lugano, Switzerland.
Abstract

An information-theoretic framework is introduced to analyze last-layer embedding, focusing on learned representations for regression tasks. We define representation-rate and derive limits on the reliability with which input-output information can be represented as is inherently determined by the input-source entropy. We further define representation capacity in a perturbed setting, and representation rate-distortion for a compressed output. We derive the achievable capacity, the achievable representation-rate, and their converse. Finally, we combine the results in a unified setting.

1 Introduction

Representation learning is one of the most investigated topics in machine learning in recent years. Previous works on representation learning focus mostly on classification downstream tasks, in which the representation ideally extracts the relevant information which is then “compressed” into the input classes (Bengio et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2020; Ben-Shaul et al., 2023; Shwartz Ziv and LeCun, 2024; Luthra et al., 2025). Neural collapse (Papyan et al., 2020) is the observed phenomena that the representation of the training data (last layer training activations) collapses to a single representation for every class.

In this work, we focus on significant observations regarding the representation latent space in regression tasks. First, we observe that class-oriented collapsed representations are not necessarily advantageous for downstream regression tasks. We then proceed to analyze the representation information-theoretic characteristics. We establish representation rate theorem for learned representations of bijective mappings (Theorem 6). We further introduce representation capacity for learned representations under degraded or perturbed input environment as the maximal operational rate in bits per input (model-use) symbol at which information can be represented with arbitrarily low probability of error (Theorem 8). We continue to investigate representation rate-distortion in a compressed-output setting (Theorem 12). Lastly, we combine the results for a setting where both the input is noisy and the output is compressed (Theorem 13).

Remark 1.

Note that despite obvious resemblance, there are major differences between Shannon’s source coding and channel coding in communication theory (Shannon, 1948; Cover and Thomas, 2006) and the theory established here for learning representations. In Shannon’s source coding theory, we design an efficient sequence of symbols building the codebook, encoding information of the source, in an attempt to minimize the redundancy and compress the representation using fewer bits than in the original representation. The channel coding theorem establishes the rate at which we can transmit information over a channel with as little error as possible, inherently describing the maximum possible efficiency of error-correcting methods depending on the level of degradation imposed by the channel. Here, however, we have a given input-representation, which we could in principle modify, and a given structure for the embedding-representation (dimension and maximum number of bits per point-value) often determined by the designer of the neural network, and we are attempting to analyze the limits of the learned representation and its efficiency and reliability. The input to the model encoding the original sequence into its corresponding representation may be a degraded measurement contaminated by (physical) noise and/or digital noise (e.g., quantization noise, numerical errors). Alternatively the inputs may also be augmented views and/or transformations of a source signal, still corresponding with a shared embedding and the same output. As indicated above the representation does not necessarily compress the data, nor does it necessarily correct for “channel” ambiguities caused by noise, varying measurements, et cetera. Thus, our goal is to reach a better understanding of the structure learned and to investigate the fundamental limitations imposed by the representation design, which in turn can shed light on the design of more efficient learning models.

Capacity in neural networks.

We note that in the context of neural networks the term capacity is used for different meanings. To name a few, the term neuronal capacity (Baldi and Vershynin, 2018) is defined as the logarithm of the size (or volume) of the hypothesis class (i.e., number of functions a neural architecture can implement). The capacity of feedforward neural networks (Baldi and Vershynin, 2019) defines cardinal capacity analogously. That is, the number of distinct functions (or with continuous weights, volume of function space) for feedforward nets of linear threshold gates. Memory capacity (Vershynin, 2020) refers to the ability to memorize arbitrary labels as a function of architecture parameters (layers and activations).

2 Background and Related Work

Recent works (Tishby and Zaslavsky, 2015; Shwartz-Ziv and Tishby, 2017; Shwartz-Ziv et al., 2018; Kawaguchi et al., 2023; Shwartz Ziv and LeCun, 2024) introduced the information bottleneck (IB) principle in the context of supervised learning and demonstrated that the convergence of DNNs’ layers follows the IB optimal bound. The IB principle assumes that an optimal representation would capture the relevant features, and compress the input by dismissing the irrelevant parts which do not contribute to the prediction. Shwartz-Ziv et al. (2018) show that for a high dimensional input and typical input sequences, the mutual information up to a representation level (layer) TT controls the generalization gap.

In previous work (Pereg, 2023a), we derived theoretical bounds of sample complexity, based on the information-theoretic asymptotic equipartition property (AEP) (Cover and Thomas, 2006). We showed that there exists a relatively small set that can empirically represent the input-output data distribution for learning and we formulated the relationship between the sample complexity, the empirical risk and the generalization error based on the typical-set properties.

Hereafter, we use the notation xnx^{n} to denote a sequence x1,x2,…,xnx_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n}, and 𝐱∈𝒳n×1\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}^{n\times 1} to denote a vector with nn entries. In information theory, a stationary stochastic process unu^{n} taking values in some finite alphabet 𝒰\mathcal{U} is called a source. More often than not, communication theory refers to discrete memoryless sources (DMS) (Kramer and others, 2008; Cover and Thomas, 2006). However, in many practical applications, signals, or local sections of them (such as image patches), can be modeled as ergodic sources belonging to some probability distribution forming statistical dependencies (e.g., a Markov random field (MRF) (Weiss and Freeman, 2007)) describing the relations between data points in close spatial or temporal proximity. To briefly summarize the AEP for ergodic sources with memory (Austin, 2017), although the formal definition of ergodic process is somewhat complex, the general idea is simple: “In an ergodic process, every sequence that is produced by the process is the same in statistical properties” (Shannon, 1948). The symbol frequencies obtained from particular sequences generated by the process, approach a definite statistical limit, as the lengths of the sequences is increased. More formally, we assume an ergodic source with memory that emits nn symbols from a discrete and finite alphabet 𝒰\mathcal{U}, with probability PU​(u1,u2,…,un)P_{U}(u_{1},u_{2},...,u_{n}). We recall a theorem (Breiman, 1957), here without proof.

Theorem 1 (Entropy and Ergodic Theory (Breiman, 1957)).

Let (un)n∈ℤ(u_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} be a stationary ergodic process ranging over a finite alphabet 𝒰\mathcal{U}, then there is a constant HH, defining the entropy rate of the source,

H(U)=limn→∞−1nlog2PU(u1,…,un).H(U)=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}-\frac{1}{n}\log_{2}P_{U}(u_{1},...,u_{n}). (1)

Intuitively, when we observe an ergodic source with memory over several entries, the uncertainty grows more slowly as nn grows, because once we know the previous source’s entries, the dependencies reduce the overall conditional uncertainty. The entropy rate HH, which represents the average uncertainty converges as the number of entries grows. This, of course, makes sense, as it is known that H⁡(X,Y)≤H⁡(X)+H⁡(Y)H(X,Y)\leq H(X)+H(Y). In other words, the uncertainty of a joint event is less than or equal to the sum of the individual uncertainties. The generalization of the AEP to arbitrary ergodic sources is as following (McMillan, 1953).

Theorem 2 (Shannon McMillan (AEP)(McMillan, 1953)).

For ϵ>0\epsilon>0, the typical set AϵnA^{n}_{\epsilon} with respect to the ergodic process PU​(u)P_{U}(u) is the set of sequences 𝐮=(u1,u2,…,un)∈𝒰n\mathbf{u}=(u_{1},u_{2},...,u_{n})\in\mathcal{U}^{n} obeying

  1. 1.

    limn→∞Pr[𝐮∈Aϵn]=1\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathrm{Pr}[\mathbf{u}\in A^{n}_{\epsilon}]=1.

  2. 2.

    2−n⁡(H+ϵ)≤PU​(𝐮)≤2−n⁡(H−ϵ)2^{-n(H+\epsilon)}\leq P_{U}(\mathbf{u})\leq 2^{-n(H-\epsilon)}.

  3. 3.

    (1−ϵ)​2n⁡(H−ϵ)≤|Aϵn|≤2n⁡(H+ϵ)(1-\epsilon)2^{n(H-\epsilon)}\leq|A^{n}_{\epsilon}|\leq 2^{n(H+\epsilon)}, for nn sufficiently large.

|A||A| denotes the number of elements in the set AA, and Pr⁡[𝒜]\mathrm{Pr}[\mathcal{A}] denotes the probability of the event 𝒜\mathcal{A} .

In other words, if we draw a random sequence (u1,u2,…,un)(u_{1},u_{2},...,u_{n}), when nn is large enough, the typical set occurs approximately with probability 1. All elements of the typical set AϵnA^{n}_{\epsilon} are approximately equally probable, and the number of elements of the typical set is approximately 2n​H2^{nH}. This property is called the asymptotic equipartition property (AEP). In information theory the AEP is considered as the analog of the law of large numbers (Cover and Thomas, 2006). The notion of a typical sequence was first introduced in 1948 by Shannon in his paper “A Mathematical Theory of Communication” (Shannon, 1948). Intuitively, the typical sequences unu^{n} are the sequences whose empirical probability mass function is close to PU​(⋅)P_{U}(\cdot).

The above results lead to further information-theoretic interpretations and insights, in relation with channel coding and source coding. Notably, the capacity of a channel defines the optimal transmission rate of communication over a channel PY|X​(y|x)P_{Y|X}(y|x). Shannon’s channel coding theorem (Shannon, 1948) states that channel capacity is C⁡(PY|X)=maxPX⁡I⁡(X,Y)C(P_{Y|X})=\max_{P_{X}}I(X;Y). In rate-distortion theory, we are trying to compress the source input under a constraint on the distortion. The optimal compression rate is R⁡(D)=minPX^|X⁡I⁡(X,X^)R(D)=\min_{P_{\hat{X}|X}}I(X;\hat{X}) s.t. E​d​(x^,x)≤D\ Ed(\hat{x},x)\leq D, where xx is the source, x^\hat{x} is the decoded signal, d⁡(x^,x)d(\hat{x},x) is a distortion measure and DD is a given distortion. Thus, in channel transmission, we wish to ﬁnd the largest set of codewords that have a large minimum distance between codewords, whereas in rate-distortion, we try to ﬁnd the smallest set of codewords that covers the entire space (Cover and Thomas, 2006). So far, the direct connection with representation learning has been an open problem. In the general neural-network problem setting, given an input-output distribution, we are trying to design a system that captures the mapping between them, by learning from fewer examples as possible (lower sample complexity). We have previously shown that the generalization error bound depends on the sample complexity relative to a given input-output mutual information (Pereg, 2023a). In this work we focus on characterization of information-theoretic properties of learned representations particularly in regression tasks, and establishing bounds determining possible implications in this context.

3 Preliminaries

3.1 Notations

Let X∈𝒳n×1X\in\mathcal{X}^{n\times 1}, Y∈𝒴n×1Y\in\mathcal{Y}^{n\times 1}, and V∈𝒱d×1V\in\mathcal{V}^{d\times 1} be random variables that obey stationary and ergodic probability distributions, and have a stationary coupling (Gray, 2009) 11 1 A stationary random process is one for which the probabilities of an event are the same regardless of when it occurs (Gray, 2009)..We consider a practical setting where XX, YY and VV are continuous random variables represented in a ﬁnite precision machine where both XX, YY and VV are quantized into a ﬁnite number of discrete values. We denote the joint probability mass function of XX and YY as PX,Y​(x,y)P_{X,Y}(x,y), and their corresponding mutual information is deﬁned as I(X;Y)=𝒟(PX,Y(x,y)||PX(x)PY(y))≥0I(X;Y)=\mathcal{D}(P_{X,Y}(x,y)||P_{X}(x)P_{Y}(y))\geq 0, where we have used the standard notation 𝒟(p||q)≜∑P(u)logP⁡(u)Q⁡(u)\mathcal{D}(p||q)\triangleq\sum P(u)\log\frac{P(u)}{Q(u)} for the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the probability mass functions PP and QQ. Namely, in a discrete setting,

I⁡(X,Y)=∑x,yPX,Y​(x,y)​log​PX,Y​(x,y)PX​(x)​PY​(y).I(X;Y)=\sum_{x,y}P_{X,Y}(x,y)\mathrm{log}\frac{P_{X,Y}(x,y)}{P_{X}(x)P_{Y}(y)}. (2)

Equivalently, we assume a sample space that is a set Ψ\Psi of paired objects Ψ={𝐱i,𝐯i}i=1m\Psi=\{\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{v}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}, where 𝐱i∈𝒳n×1\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathcal{X}^{n\times 1} are sampled from PX​(x)P_{X}(x) and paired with 𝐯i∈𝒱d×1\mathbf{v}_{i}\in\mathcal{V}^{d\times 1} by a deterministic or stochastic mapping as ground truth. The notations 𝐱\mathbf{x} and XX are used below interchangeably.

3.2 Classification vs Regression

Consider a mixture model PX​(𝐱)=∑k=1MPθ​(θk)​PX|θ​(𝐱|θk)P_{X}(\mathbf{x})=\sum^{M}_{k=1}P_{\theta}(\theta_{k})P_{X|\theta}(\mathbf{x}|\theta_{k}), such that 𝐱∈𝒳n×1\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}^{n\times 1}, and θ\theta represents one of MM underlying classes. We further assume a forward regression model PV|X​(𝐯|𝐱)P_{V|X}(\mathbf{v}|\mathbf{x}) independent of θ\theta. Accordingly, PV​(𝐯)=∑k=1MPθ​(θk)​PV|θ​(𝐯|θk)P_{V}(\mathbf{v})=\sum^{M}_{k=1}P_{\theta}(\theta_{k})P_{V|\theta}(\mathbf{v}|\theta_{k}). Denote ℱ:𝒳n→𝒵q\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{X}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}^{q} as a function that maps input samples to qq-dimensional embedding vectors 𝐳i∈𝒵q×1\mathbf{z}_{i}\in\mathcal{Z}^{q\times 1}. The embedding function ℱ\mathcal{F} is trained via supervised learning or self-supervised contrastive learning, using a dataset Ψ={(𝐱i,𝐯i,ci)}i=1m\Psi=\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{v}_{i},c_{i})\}^{m}_{i=1}, where cic_{i} is the corresponding class label. In the self-supervised training the model only learns from the inputs {𝐱i}i=1m\{\mathbf{x}_{i}\}^{m}_{i=1}, but not the corresponding class labels cic_{i}.

Proposition 3 (Class-oriented representation-collapse for regression).

Collapsed representations learned by employing self-supervised contrastive learning align with downstream classification tasks, but are inadequate for regression tasks. That said, clustered representations that have not fully-collapsed to their mean, could still have sufficient variability and could potentially reliably represent the different output signals in every class.

Proof.

Papyan et al. (2020) showed that in classification deep neural networks, the top-layer feature embeddings of training samples of each class tend to cluster around respective class means, which are maximally distant from each other. This phenomenon is generally considered desirable for classification tasks and segmentation 22 2 segmentation is considered here as classification of patches tasks because max-margin classifiers exhibit better generalization guarantees (Ben-Shaul et al., 2023; Anthony and Bartlett, 2009), and clustered embedding spaces are useful for few-shot transfer learning (Goldblum et al., 2020; Galanti et al., 2022).

Previous work (Luthra et al., 2025) showed that when ℱ\mathcal{F} is a global minimizer of the negatives-only supervised contrastive loss,

ℒNSCL=−1K2​m∑l​1,l​2=1K∑i=1mlog(exp⁡(sim⁡(𝐳il​1,𝐳il2))∑l3=1K∑i≠jexp⁡(sim⁡(𝐳il​1,𝐳jl3))),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NSCL}}=-\frac{1}{K^{2}m}\sum^{K}_{l1,l2=1}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log\Bigg(\frac{\mathrm{exp}(\mathrm{sim}(\mathbf{z}^{l1}_{i},\mathbf{z}^{l_{2}}_{i}))}{\sum^{K}_{l_{3}=1}\sum_{i\neq j}\mathrm{exp}(\mathrm{sim}(\mathbf{z}^{l1}_{i},\mathbf{z}^{l_{3}}_{j}))}\Bigg), (3)

where sim⁡(𝐱1,𝐱2)=<𝐱1,𝐱2>‖𝐱1‖2​‖𝐱2‖2\mathrm{sim}(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2})=\frac{<\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2}>}{\|\mathbf{x}_{1}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{x}_{2}\|_{2}} is the cosine similarity function, and 𝐱il\mathbf{x}_{i}^{l} and 𝐳il\mathbf{z}_{i}^{l} denote an input augmentation and its corresponding feature vector, the obtained representations obey:

    Augmentation Collapse: For each class, and for every pair l1,l2≤Kl_{1},l_{2}\leq K, we have 𝐳il1=𝐳il2\mathbf{z}^{l_{1}}_{i}=\mathbf{z}^{l_{2}}_{i}.

  2. 2.

    Within-Class Collapse: For any two samples 𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i} and 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j} with the same label (ci=cjc_{i}=c_{j}), their representations coincide: 𝐳i=𝐳j\mathbf{z}_{i}=\mathbf{z}_{j}. Namely, each class has a unique class embedding.

  3. 3.

    Simplex Equiangular Tight Frame: Let {μ1,…,μM}\{\mu_{1},...,\mu_{M}\} denote the set of class-center embeddings. Under the assumption that 𝐳∈ℝq\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{q}, these vectors form a simplex ETF in ℝq\mathbb{R}^{q}; specifically, they satisfy ∑c=1Mμc=0\sum^{M}_{c=1}\mu_{c}=0, ‖μc‖=‖μc′‖\|\mu_{c}\|=\|\mu_{c^{\prime}}\|, <μc,μc′>=−‖μc‖22M−1∀c≠c′<\mu_{c},\mu_{c^{\prime}}>=-\frac{\|\mu_{c}\|_{2}^{2}}{M-1}\ \forall c\neq c^{\prime}.

Luthra et al. (2025) show that self-supervised decoupled contrastive loss (Yeh et al., 2022) follows similar behavior to the supervised model and thus exhibits neural collapse. Now, consider ℱ\mathcal{F} is used for the regression task by adding a fully connected linear decoder and using the learned features. That is 𝐯^=A​ℱ​(𝐱)\hat{\mathbf{v}}=A\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}). For a specific class, the regression outputs 𝐯ik∼p⁡(𝐯|θ=θk)\mathbf{v}_{i}^{k}\sim p(\mathbf{v}|\theta=\theta_{k}) within the same class θk\theta_{k} vary:

𝐯ki≠𝐯kj,i≠j,k=1,…,M.\mathbf{v}^{k}_{i}\neq\mathbf{v}^{k}_{j},\quad i\neq j,\ k=1,...,M. (4)

Denote the class unique embedding as 𝐳ck\mathbf{z}_{c_{k}}. Since the learned features collapse, 𝐳i|θk=𝐳j|θk=𝐳ck\mathbf{z}_{i}|\theta_{k}=\mathbf{z}_{j}|\theta_{k}=\mathbf{z}_{c_{k}}, all outputs within the same class collapse too, 𝐯i^k=A​ℱ​(𝐱i)=A​𝐳ck=𝐯j^k\hat{\mathbf{v}_{i}}^{k}=A\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}_{i})=A\mathbf{z}_{c_{k}}=\hat{\mathbf{v}_{j}}^{k}. This is true for any decoder 𝒢⁡(⋅)\mathcal{G}(\cdot) regardless of its architecture as all features in the same class are identical. ∎

To a certain extent, this is a known property of classification neural nets, as the only information that must be preserved throughout the layers of the net is the class of the input signal. Accordingly the dimension of the representation is significantly smaller than the input dimensions, that is q<<nq<<n. For example in ResNet-50 the input 𝐱∈ℝ224×224×3\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{224\times 224\times 3}, thus n≈218n\approx 2^{18}, whereas 𝐳∈ℝ2048×1\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{2048\times 1}, and q=211q=2^{11} (He et al., 2016). In other words, it is assumed that the encoder compresses the input and maintains only the relevant information to distinguish between one class to another.

In regressions tasks, such as image-to-image translation, architectures are normally over-parametrized. Although in certain architectures the encoder contracts (such as Deep STORM (Nehme et al., 2018) and denoising autoencoder (Rumelhart et al., 1985)), in others the information from the input is passed directly to the decoder (e.g., UNET (Ronneberger et al., 2015)). In few-shot RNN (Pereg et al., 2020; Pereg, 2023b; Pereg, 2024) the input 𝐱∈ℝ30×1\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{30\times 1}, thus n≈25n\approx 2^{5}, whereas 𝐳∈ℝ1000×1\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{1000\times 1}, and q≈210q\approx 2^{10}. It is indicated that q>>nq>>n and that the representation is sparse. In those tasks the model must preserve all the information necessary to transform the input to the output space, and only discard noise and irrelevant information (in the sense that everything that is not an event - is noise). In early autoencoder designs (Rumelhart et al., 1985; Kramer, 1991; Baldi and Hornik, 1989) the hidden layer is significantly smaller than the input size, (e.g., input of size 28×2828\times 28 is mapped to 32 or 64 values) with the intention to compress the input and/or project it onto a lower-dimensional representation. Whereas modern denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al., 2008) are highly over-parametrized, e.g., an input of size 28×2828\times 28 is mapped to 1000-2000 sigmoid units. In machine learning literature, the embedding space is usually assumed to be continuous and finite, such that 𝐳∈ℝq,‖𝐳‖≤1\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{q},\ \|\mathbf{z}\|\leq 1. Here, we will take a different approach.

Confusion with compression and rate-distortion theory.

The change of length of the block and the size of the alphabet, along with repeated abuse of terminology in the data-science literature, created a misleading misconception that the representation is always a compressed representation of the input. Whereas in most regression tasks each input must have a unique representation and a unique output, thus the ‘‘codebook” size of the embedding must have sufficient ‘‘capacity”33 3 The term capacity is slightly abused here. .

4 Representation Capacity

Channel Capacity

“What do we mean when we say that A communicates with B? We mean that the physical acts of A have induced a desired physical state in B. This transfer of information is a physical process and therefore is subject to the uncontrollable ambient noise and imperfections of the physical signaling process itself. The communication is successful if the receiver B and the transmitter A agree on what was sent.” (Cover and Thomas, 2006). “A communication channel is a system in which the output depends probabilistically on its input. It is characterized by a probability transition matrix p⁡(y|x)p(y|x) that determines the conditional distribution of the output given the input” (Cover and Thomas, 2006). In communication, channel capacity represents the maximum number of distinguishable signals for nn uses of a communication channel.

Representation Capacity

In our setting, that is, in representation learning, we assume a signal 𝐱∈𝒳n×1\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}^{n\times 1} that is an original ground truth signal (source) passing through a system, where the output of the system (channel) is the measurement 𝐲∈𝒴n×1\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{Y}^{n\times 1}, which is the input to a neural net, to be represented by distinguishable 𝐳∈𝒵q×1\mathbf{z}\in\mathcal{Z}^{q\times 1} in the embedding space (as illustrated in Fig. 2). Assuming that the embedding should represent distinguishable source signals 𝐱\mathbf{x}, we ask: What is the maximum number of distinguishable signals per each input point value (pixel)? For a system with source signal XX and output YY, we can deﬁne the representation capacity 𝒞\mathcal{C} by

𝒞=maxPX​(𝐱)⁡I⁡(X,Y).\mathcal{C}=\max_{P_{X}(\mathbf{x})}I(X;Y). (5)

Later we show that the representation capacity is the maximum rate at which information can be reliably represented and recovered by the representation with a vanishingly low probability of error.

Let us first consider a channel-free setting as illustrated in Fig. 1. Let 𝐱∈𝒳n×1\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}^{n\times 1} be an input signal, such that |𝒳||\mathcal{X}| is the cardinality of the input alphabet. For example, in most image-related datasets the pixel values are originally integers xi∈[0,1,…,255]x_{i}\in[0,1,...,255] (normally normalized to the range [−1,1][-1,1] before further processing), thus |𝒳|=28|\mathcal{X}|=2^{8}. Let us assume a training set Ψ={𝐱i,𝐯i}i=1m\Psi=\{\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{v}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}, where 𝐱i∈𝒳n×1\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathcal{X}^{n\times 1} are sampled from PX​(𝐱)P_{X}(\mathbf{x}) and paired with 𝐯i∈𝒱d×1\mathbf{v}_{i}\in\mathcal{V}^{d\times 1} by some function as ground truth. The learning system is trained to output a prediction rule ℱ:𝒳n→𝒱d\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{X}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}^{d}. Assume an algorithm that trains the predictor by minimizing the training error (empirical error or empirical risk).

Bijective transformation

For the sake of the following theoretical analysis we restrict the mapping ℱ:𝒳n→𝒱d\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{X}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}^{d} to be a bijective (invertible) function. Namely, for every vdv^{d}, there is a single xnx^{n} such that vd=g⁡(xn)v^{d}=g(x^{n}), and for every xnx^{n}, there is a single vdv^{d} such that xn=g−1​(vd)x^{n}=g^{-1}(v^{d}). In other words, every element vdv^{d} is the image of one element of xnx^{n}. It is required that xnx^{n} is unique. As we established in the Proposition 3, for every two distinguishable outputs 𝐯i≠𝐯j\mathbf{v}_{i}\neq\mathbf{v}_{j}, the corresponding embedding must be distinguishable too, 𝐳i≠𝐳j\mathbf{z}_{i}\neq\mathbf{z}_{j}. Since every input must have an output, by assumption |𝒳|n≤|𝒱|d|\mathcal{X}|^{n}\leq|\mathcal{V}|^{d}.

The Embedding Space

More often than not, the embedding space is assumed to be a floating point in a continuous space such that 𝐳∈ℝq,0≤|𝐳|≤1\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{q},0\leq|\mathbf{z}|\leq 1. Here, we will assume a finite digit representation such that 𝐳∈𝒵q\mathbf{z}\in\mathcal{Z}^{q}, where |𝒵|<<∞|\mathcal{Z}|<<\infty.

Considering the first classification network for MNIST LeNet-5 (LeCun et al., 2002), the input images of size 32×3232\times 32, when xi∈[0,1,…​255]x_{i}\in[0,1,...255]. Therefore, |𝒳|n=2561024=28192|\mathcal{X}|^{n}=256^{1024}=2^{8192}. For the sake of simplification we will assume ‖zi‖≤1\|z_{i}\|\leq 1 represented by float32, and a rough estimate of |𝒵|≈231|\mathcal{Z}|\approx 2^{31} quantized numbers in this range. (If one is using TensorFloat-32, |𝒵|≈210|\mathcal{Z}|\approx 2^{10}). It is often assumed that the representation (feature) space reduces the dimensionality of the input because usually n>>qn>>q. Although |𝒵|>>|𝒳||\mathcal{Z}|>>|\mathcal{X}|, in many cases the embedding space does not have the “capacity” to represent every point in the input ambient space, including those which are not part of the support of input manifold (e.g., input manifold of digits, natural images, etc.). For example, if q=128q=128, then we can only have at most |𝒵|q=231∗128=23968|\mathcal{Z}|^{q}=2^{31*128}=2^{3968} representations. For the embedding space to have as many distinguable points as potentially in the full input ambient space |𝒳|n=28192|\mathcal{X}|^{n}=2^{8192} we would require that |𝒵|=264|\mathcal{Z}|=2^{64}, which is unrealistic in practice. Accordingly, the Data Manifold Hypothesis (Olah, 2014) postulates that real-world datasets lie on a manifold whose intrinsic dimensionality is considerably lower than the ambient input space. While numerous models can completely fit training data, in order for the model to generalize well, it likely learns meaningful representations of this underlying manifold.

That said, we note that saying that the embedding space is compressing the input is generally a misleading statement. For example, if an input image patch of size 64×6464\times 64 where pixels are integers in the range [0,255][0,255], is represented in the embedding space in a vector 𝐳∈𝒵1024×1\mathbf{z}\in\mathcal{Z}^{1024\times 1} represented as a floating point with 32 bits. Then each input pixel is represented by 8 bits in the embedding space, which is the same number of bits per symbol as in the input representation space. If the input image patch is smaller, say of size 16×1616\times 16 where pixels are integers in the range [0,255][0,255], represented in the embedding space in a vector 𝐳∈𝒵1024×1\mathbf{z}\in\mathcal{Z}^{1024\times 1} represented in as a floating point with 32 bits, then each input pixel is represented by 128 bits in the embedding space which is a significantly larger number of bits.

The Embedding Separation Distance

When the model is a bijective function every input has a corresponding distinguisbale representation point in the z-domain. Every input has an embedding that is separable from other embeddings by a qq-dimensional sphere. We will refer to the radius of that sphere as the embedding separation distance denoted by ε\varepsilon.

Embedding Continuity

Let us assume the mapping ℱ:𝒳n→𝒵q\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{X}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}^{q} is Lipschitz continuous44 4 Only required for Theorem 10 with a constant Kc>0K_{c}>0

‖𝐳i−𝐳j‖‖𝐱i−𝐱j‖≤Kc,∀𝐳∈𝒵q,𝐱∈𝒳n,\frac{\|\mathbf{z}_{i}-\mathbf{z}_{j}\|}{\|\mathbf{x}_{i}-\mathbf{x}_{j}\|}\leq K_{c},\quad\forall\mathbf{z}\in\mathcal{Z}^{q},\ \mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}^{n}, (6)

where ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| denotes a norm. Thus requiring that the target function is locally smooth, i.e., if we perturb the input 𝐱\mathbf{x} slightly the embedding does not change much.

5 Theoretical Bounds

We first assume a supervised learning algorithm with a training set Ψ\Psi, where the input xnx^{n} is sampled from an unknown distribution PXP_{X} and paired with vdv^{d} by some target function g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot), to learn a predictor hΨ:𝒳n→𝒱dh_{\Psi}:\mathcal{X}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}^{d}. The algorithm is designed to yield a model hΨh_{\Psi} that would ideally minimize the error over an unknown PX,V​(⋅)P_{X,V}(\cdot) over 𝒳n×𝒱d\mathcal{X}^{n}\times\mathcal{V}^{d}, as the true error is not available to the learner. The subscript Ψ\Psi emphasizes that the output predictor depends on Ψ\Psi. The learning process minimizes the empirical risk

ℒΨ​(hΨ)=1m​∑i=1mℓ⁡(hΨ​(𝐱i),𝐯i),\mathcal{L}_{\Psi}(h_{\Psi})=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\ell(h_{\Psi}(\mathbf{x}_{i}),\mathbf{v}_{i}), (7)

where 0≤ℓ⁡(𝐯^,𝐯)≤10\leq\ell(\hat{\mathbf{v}},\mathbf{v})\leq 1 is some loss function. The empirical error over the training set at the end of the training, for the specific trained predictor hΨh_{\Psi} is ℒΨ​(hΨ)≤Δm<<1\mathcal{L}_{\Psi}(h_{\Psi})\leq\Delta_{m}<<1. The true error, or the generalization error, in this setting is

ℒ⁡(hΨ)=E(x,v)∼PX,V​[ℓ⁡(hΨ​(𝐱),𝐯)],\mathcal{L}(h_{\Psi})=E_{(x,v)\sim P_{X,V}}\big[\ell\big(h_{\Psi}(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{v}\big)\big], (8)

where E(x,v)∼PX,V​[⋅]E_{(x,v)\sim P_{X,V}}[\cdot] denotes the expectation over PX,VP_{X,V}. The ability of a trained learner to generalize well is guaranteed by the upper bound on the generalization error, ℒ⁡(hΨ)≤Δ\mathcal{L}(h_{\Psi})\leq\Delta.

Definition 4 (Embedding Code).

A source code Cz​(x)C_{\mathrm{z}}(x) for a random source sequence xnx^{n} is a mapping Cz​(x):𝒳n→𝒵qC_{\mathrm{z}}(x):\mathcal{X}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}^{q}.

Definition 5 (Embedding representation rate).

A source code Cz​(x)C_{\mathrm{z}}(x) for a random source sequence xnx^{n} and a rate of ℛ\mathcal{R} bits per source symbol is a mapping Cz​(x):𝒳n→𝒵qC_{\mathrm{z}}(x):\mathcal{X}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}^{q}. The embedding produces ℛ\mathcal{R} bits per input symbol. Namely, 2n​ℛ=|𝒵|q2^{n\mathcal{R}}=|\mathcal{Z}|^{q}. Denote, 𝒬z=log2⁡|𝒵|q\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{z}}=\log_{2}|\mathcal{Z}|^{q}. Therefore,

ℛ=q​log2​|𝒵|n=𝒬zn.\mathcal{R}=\frac{q\log_{2}|\mathcal{Z}|}{n}=\frac{\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{z}}}{n}. (9)

For example, in the above MNIST LeNet-5 (LeCun et al., 2002), ℛ=128​log2⁡(231)32∗32=3.875\mathcal{R}=\frac{128\log_{2}(2^{31})}{32*32}=3.875 bits per input pixel. As stated above, the input pixels were originally represented by 8 bits per pixel. Therefore, the embedding does not have the ‘‘capacity”55 5 the use of the term capacity here, as in most machine learning literature, is slightly misleading. to represent every possible input in the full support (input ambient space) with a distinguishable representation, however it may cover the empirical support defined by the typical set, as described in Theorem 6 below.

5.1 Representation rate in the noise-free setting

Theorem 6 (Embedding representation rate for a bijective mapping).

Let g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot) be a deterministic bijective function. Let Ψ={{𝐱i,𝐯i}i=1m:𝐱i∼PX,𝐯i=g(𝐱i),𝐱i∈𝒳n×1,𝐯i∈𝒱d×1}\Psi=\big\{\{\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{v}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}:\mathbf{x}_{i}\sim P_{X},\quad\mathbf{v}_{i}=g(\mathbf{x}_{i}),\ \mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathcal{X}^{n\times 1},\ \mathbf{v}_{i}\in\mathcal{V}^{d\times 1}\big\} be a training set that is generated by randomly drawing samples from PXP_{X} and labeling them by the target function g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot). Let hΨ:𝒳n→𝒱dh_{\Psi}:\mathcal{X}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}^{d} be a trained predictor such that, hΨ=ℱ⁡(𝒢⁡(𝐱))h_{\Psi}=\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{x})), where ℱ:𝒳n→𝒵q\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{X}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}^{q}, and 𝒢:𝒵q→𝒱d\mathcal{G}:\mathcal{Z}^{q}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}^{d}. For nn sufficiently large, if the embedding space obeys

𝒬z≥n​H​(X),\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{z}}\geq nH(X), (10)

in other words,

ℛ≥H⁡(X),\mathcal{R}\geq H(X), (11)

then there exists a trained predictor 𝐯^=hΨ​(𝐱)=𝒢⁡(ℱ⁡(𝐱)),𝐳=ℱ⁡(𝐱)\hat{\mathbf{v}}=h_{\Psi}(\mathbf{x})=\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})),\ \mathbf{z}=\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}), such that the probability of error Pe≜Pr[hΨ(𝐱)≠𝐯]→0,∀𝐱∼PXP_{e}\triangleq Pr[h_{\Psi}(\mathbf{x})\neq\mathbf{v}]\rightarrow 0,\ \forall\mathbf{x}\sim P_{X}. That is, the generalization error ℒ⁡(hΨ)→0\mathcal{L}(h_{\Psi})\rightarrow 0.

Conversely, if ℛ<H⁡(X)−ϵ\mathcal{R}<H(X)-\epsilon then the probability of error
Pe≜Pr[hΨ(𝐱)≠𝐯]→1,∀𝐱∼PXP_{e}\triangleq Pr[h_{\Psi}(\mathbf{x})\neq\mathbf{v}]\rightarrow 1,\ \forall\mathbf{x}\sim P_{X}.

Proof. See Appendix A.

Remark 2.

The proof deduces that for every 𝐱∈Aϵn​(PX)\mathbf{x}\in A^{n}_{\epsilon}(P_{X}) there is a corresponding unique output 𝐯\mathbf{v}, hence

d​log2​|𝒱|≥n​H​(X).d\log_{2}|\mathcal{V}|\geq nH(X). (12)

Note that assuming that all inputs are equiprobable (either on the basis of the AEP, or by the nature of the input distribution), and thus all representations are equiprobable, H⁡(Z)=𝒬zH(Z)=\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{z}}, which is the maximum entropy of the representation achieved when all possible representations are uniformly distributed.

Remark 3.

Note that these theorems are independent of the hypothesis class of hΨ​(𝐱)h_{\Psi}(\mathbf{x}). That is, if the rate is insufficient at the representation level, no architecture can compensate for that.

5.2 Representation rate in a noisy environment

Now, let us assume a discrete source PX​(⋅)P_{X}(\cdot) that emits i.i.d sequences xnx^{n} of symbols (for example: patches in an image, frames of an audio signal, etc.), the estimator has access only to the observed signal yny^{n}, which is a transformed form of xnx^{n} according to the conditional distribution PY|X​(𝐲|𝐱)P_{Y|X}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}). For example, yny^{n} could be a degraded signal originating in xnx^{n}, as a result of additive noise, linear or nonlinear degradation and/or quantization, where the relationship between xnx^{n} and yny^{n} could be linear or non-linear, with or without additive noise, such that generally yn=u⁡(xn)+e⁡(xn)y^{n}=u(x^{n})+e(x^{n}), where u⁡(⋅)u(\cdot) and e⁡(⋅)e(\cdot) are functions of xnx^{n}. Indeed, most real-life practical signal-to-signal models assume an input measurement 𝐲\mathbf{y} that could be noisy and/or degraded, yet the output should correspond with the central (and/or average) clean signal, denoted here as 𝐱\mathbf{x} (e.g., EMG to speech (Hou et al., 2024), medical imaging reconstruction (Young et al., 2024), speech to text (Baevski et al., 2020), and so on) (see Figure 2). Importantly, PY|X(⋅|𝐱)P_{Y|X}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) corresponds with any heuristic stage generating a noisy or distorted or transformed measurement from the original ground truth 𝐱\mathbf{x}, when 𝐲\mathbf{y} are the inputs to the neural net. This stage can also correspond with any preprocessing stage applied to the signal, which yields the input to the neural net, such as: rescaling, normalization, clipping and quantization, as well as any augmentations of the input, such as different views from different angles, different contrast, colors, etc., which are to be mapped to the same output 𝐯\mathbf{v}, thus correspond with the same source 𝐱\mathbf{x}. For the sake of the following theoretical analysis we restrict the learned mapping hΨ:𝒴n→𝒱dh_{\Psi}:\mathcal{Y}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}^{d} to be a surjective function. Namely, for every vdv^{d}, there is a yny^{n} such that h⁡(yn)=vdh(y^{n})=v^{d}. In other words, every element vdv^{d} is the image of at least one element of yny^{n}. It is not required that yny^{n} be unique. The relation 𝐱→𝐯\mathbf{x}\rightarrow\mathbf{v} is a bijection, and the input to the estimator is 𝐲∼PY|X(⋅|𝐱)\mathbf{y}\sim P_{Y|X}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}). In the presence of noise this condition can only be met in practice if the noise’s power is under a certain threshold. In an inverse problem where the predictor is trained for signal restoration vd=xdv^{d}=x^{d} and given ydy^{d}, we produce an estimate x^d\hat{x}^{d} (n=d), however, the following proofs are not restricted to this framework. Further assume a training set Ψ={𝐲i,𝐯i}i=1m\Psi=\{\mathbf{y}_{i},\mathbf{v}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}, where 𝐲i∈𝒴n×1\mathbf{y}_{i}\in\mathcal{Y}^{n\times 1} are sampled from PY|XP_{Y|X} and paired with 𝐯i∈𝒱d×1\mathbf{v}_{i}\in\mathcal{V}^{d\times 1} by some function as ground truth. The learning system is trained to output a prediction rule hΨ:𝒴n→𝒱dh_{\Psi}:\mathcal{Y}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}^{d}. Assume an algorithm that trains the predictor by minimizing the training error (empirical error or empirical risk).

Definition 7 (Effective Support of the Embedding Space).

The non-zero support of the embedding of a specific model 𝐳=ℱΨ​(⋅)\mathbf{z}=\mathcal{F}_{\Psi}(\cdot) is defined as

𝒮(𝐳)={i∈{1,2,…,|𝒵|q}:𝐳i∈𝒵q,𝐳i≠𝟎}.\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{z})=\Big\{i\in\big\{1,2,...,|\mathcal{Z}|^{q}\big\}\ :\ \mathbf{z}_{i}\in\mathcal{Z}^{q},\ \mathbf{z}_{i}\neq\mathbf{0}\Big\}. (13)

We denote the cardinality of the non-zero support,

𝒬~z≜log2⁡|𝒮⁡(𝐳)|.\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}_{\mathrm{z}}\triangleq\log_{2}\big|\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{z})\big|. (14)

Let ℬx={𝐱i,i∈ℳ}\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{x}}=\{\mathbf{x}_{i},\ i\in\mathcal{M}\} be a set of distinct M=|ℳ|M=|\mathcal{M}| sequences in 𝒳n×1\mathcal{X}^{n\times 1} that are resolved from the inputs 𝐲\mathbf{y} and mapped to their corresponding 𝐯i\mathbf{v}_{i}, and M≜2n​ℛM\triangleq 2^{n\mathcal{R}}.

Theorem 8 (Embedding Capacity).

Let Ψ\Psi be a training set that is generated by randomly drawing samples from PY|XP_{Y|X} and labeling them by the target function such that, Ψ={{𝐲i,𝐯i}i=1m:𝐲i∼PY|X(⋅|𝐱),𝐱i∈𝒳n×1,𝐲i∈𝒴n×1,𝐯i∈𝒱d×1}\Psi=\big\{\{\mathbf{y}_{i},\mathbf{v}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}:\mathbf{y}_{i}\sim P_{Y|X}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}),\ \ \mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathcal{X}^{n\times 1},\ \mathbf{y}_{i}\in\mathcal{Y}^{n\times 1},\ \mathbf{v}_{i}\in\mathcal{V}^{d\times 1}\big\}. Let hΨ:𝒴n→𝒱dh_{\Psi}:\mathcal{Y}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}^{d} be a trained predictor such that, hΨ=ℱ⁡(𝒢⁡(𝐲))h_{\Psi}=\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{y})), where ℱ:𝒴n→𝒵q\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{Y}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}^{q}, and 𝒢:𝒵q→𝒱d\mathcal{G}:\mathcal{Z}^{q}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}^{d}. For nn sufficiently large, if

ℛ<I⁡(X,Y).\mathcal{R}<I(X;Y). (15)

then there exists a trained predictor hΨh_{\Psi} such that the probability of error
Pe≜Pr[hΨ(𝐲)≠𝐯]→0,∀𝐲∼PY|X(⋅|𝐱)P_{e}\triangleq Pr[h_{\Psi}(\mathbf{y})\neq\mathbf{v}]\rightarrow 0,\ \forall\mathbf{y}\sim P_{Y|X}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}).
When 𝒢\mathcal{G} is an injective mapping, the effective support of the embedding space obeys

𝒬~z<n​I​(X,Y).\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}_{\mathrm{z}}<nI(X;Y). (16)

Conversely, if Pe≜Pr[hΨ(𝐲)≠𝐯]→0,∀𝐲∼PY|X(⋅|𝐱)P_{e}\triangleq Pr[h_{\Psi}(\mathbf{y})\neq\mathbf{v}]\rightarrow 0,\ \forall\mathbf{y}\sim P_{Y|X}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}), then ℛ<I⁡(X,Y)\mathcal{R}<I(X;Y).

Proof. See Appendix B.

Remark 4.

We note that when 𝒢\mathcal{G} is injective, for a perfect representation we have H⁡(X)=H⁡(Z)=H⁡(V)H(X)=H(Z)=H(V) since the representation and the output are a bijection of the source, as well as I⁡(X,Y)=I⁡(Z,Y)=I⁡(V,Y)I(X;Y)=I(Z;Y)=I(V;Y).

Remark 5.

The term “effective support of the embedding space” refers to the non-zero support, indicating that the upper bound of 𝒬~z\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}_{\mathrm{z}} does not limit the practical utility of an embedding space of higher representation rate, but it defines its inherent limited ability to capture a limited number of representations. A representation of higher dimension, or of larger alphabet, would be able, in principle, to reliably represent more signals. Yet, the number of distinguishable signals in this setting is limited by ℛ<I⁡(X,Y)\mathcal{R}<I(X;Y). However, if 𝒢⁡(𝐳)\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{z}) is an injective mapping and the effective support 𝒬~z>n​I​(X,Y)\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}_{\mathrm{z}}>nI(X;Y), it implies that different 𝐲\mathbf{y}’s originating in the same 𝐱\mathbf{x} are mapped to different 𝐯\mathbf{v}’s, and that the mapping is erroneous.

Remark 6.

The assumption that 𝒢:𝒵q→𝒱d\mathcal{G}:\mathcal{Z}^{q}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}^{d} is an injective mapping may seem too restrictive, but recent work indicates that in regression tasks 𝒢\mathcal{G} is invertible on the collapsed latent subspace (Andriopoulos et al., 2024). It is shown that the last-layer feature vectors collapse to the subspace spanned by the dd principal components of the feature vectors, where dd is the dimension of the targets, and also to the subspace spanned by the last-layer weight vectors, comprising 𝒢\mathcal{G} in our setting.

Remark 7.

Despite the aforementioned significant differences between transmission rate in communication theory and the established theory here, and although the embedding rate does not directly capture an efficiency of error-correcting methods, it does bound the limits to which the learned model can correct for errors or the imperfections determined by the transformation PY|X(⋅|𝐱)P_{Y|X}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}). It is indicative of the extent to which the learned mapping can exploit structural redundancy to reconstruct the correct output.

Definition 9 (Representation Capacity).

The representation capacity is

𝒞=maxPX​(𝐱)⁡𝒬~z=maxPX​(𝐱)⁡I⁡(X,Y),\mathcal{C}=\max_{P_{X}(\mathbf{x})}\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}_{\mathrm{z}}=\max_{P_{X}(\mathbf{x})}\ I(X;Y), (17)

where the maximum is taken over all possible input distributions PX​(𝐱)P_{X}(\mathbf{x}).

Thus, the operational deﬁnition of representation capacity is the highest rate in bits per model-use at which information can be represented with arbitrarily low probability of error. The representation capacity inherently depends on how many input signals are to be mapped to the same embedding point.

Example 1. Consider 𝐲=𝐱+𝐞\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{e}, where 𝒳n={𝐱1,𝐱2,…,𝐱M}\mathcal{X}^{n}=\{\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2},...,\mathbf{x}_{M}\} and ℰn={𝐞1,𝐞2,…,𝐞P}\mathcal{E}^{n}=\{\mathbf{e}_{1},\mathbf{e}_{2},...,\mathbf{e}_{P}\} are independent and both uniformly distributed. Further assume that the map 𝐲→𝐱\mathbf{y}\rightarrow\mathbf{x} is surjective. Since in this case YnY^{n} is uniform on its support with PYn(yin)=1M​P,i=1,…,MPP_{Y^{n}}(y_{i}^{n})=\frac{1}{MP},\ i=1,...,MP, we have

I⁡(X,Y)=H⁡(Y)−H⁡(Y|X)=H⁡(Y)−H⁡(E)=1n​(log2⁡M​P−log2⁡P)=1n​log2​M=H⁡(X).I(X;Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)=H(Y)-H(E)=\frac{1}{n}(\log_{2}MP-\log_{2}P)=\frac{1}{n}\log_{2}M=H(X).

Example 2. Additive Gaussian noise with discrete input probability mass function. For the sake of simplicity, in this example we will consider 𝐘∈ℝn\mathbf{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. We consider a discrete random signal XnX^{n} taking values in a finite alphabet Ω⊆𝒳n\Omega\ \subseteq\mathcal{X}^{n}. The number of symbols in the constellation is |Ω|=M|\Omega|=M, with probability PXn(xin)=1M,i=1,…,MP_{X^{n}}(x_{i}^{n})=\frac{1}{M},\ i=1,...,M (Delsad, 2023). The degraded input signal YnY^{n}, where 𝐲=snr​𝐱+𝐞\mathbf{y}=\mathrm{snr}\ \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{e} and 𝐞∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)\mathbf{e}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}), is a mixture of Gaussians. Wu and Verdú (2010) show that as MM, the cardinality of XX, grows, the capacity CMC_{M} approaches 𝒞⁡(snr)=12​log⁡(1+snr)\mathcal{C}(\mathrm{snr})=\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\mathrm{snr}).

Remark 8.

In different practical settings training is sometimes executed with Ψy={𝐲i,𝐯i}i=1m\Psi_{\mathrm{y}}=\{\mathbf{y}_{i},\mathbf{v}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}, whereas in other applications the training set consists of the original source-inputs Ψx={𝐱i,𝐯i}i=1m\Psi_{\mathrm{x}}=\{\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{v}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}, while the inputs in practice are 𝐲i\mathbf{y}_{i}, i.e., perturbed or noisy measurements, and it is expected for the mapping to generalize well. The results in Theorem 8 apply to both cases, although they do not guarantee the performance of the predictor is optimal. This case-study is addressed in Theorem 10 below.

Theorem 10 (Generalization error for a noisy input).

Let g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot) be a deterministic bijective function. Let Ψx={{𝐱i,𝐯i}i=1m:𝐱i∼PX,𝐯i=g(𝐱i),𝐱i∈𝒳n×1,𝐯i∈𝒱d×1}\Psi_{\mathrm{x}}=\big\{\{\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{v}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}:\mathbf{x}_{i}\sim P_{X},\quad\mathbf{v}_{i}=g(\mathbf{x}_{i}),\ \mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathcal{X}^{n\times 1},\ \mathbf{v}_{i}\in\mathcal{V}^{d\times 1}\big\} be a training set that is generated by randomly drawing samples from PXP_{X} and labeling them by the target function g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot). Let hΨx:𝒳n→𝒱dh_{\Psi_{\mathrm{x}}}:\mathcal{X}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}^{d} be a trained predictor such that, hΨx​(𝐱)=ℱ⁡(𝒢⁡(𝐱))h_{\Psi_{\mathrm{x}}}(\mathbf{x})=\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{x})), where ℱ:𝒳n→𝒵q\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{X}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}^{q}, and 𝒢:𝒵q→𝒱d\mathcal{G}:\mathcal{Z}^{q}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}^{d}. Assume the predictor hΨx:𝒳n→𝒱dh_{\Psi_{\mathrm{x}}}:\mathcal{X}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}^{d} was trained successfully to yield ℒ⁡(hΨx)≤Δ<<1\mathcal{L}(h_{\Psi_{\mathrm{x}}})\leq\Delta<<1, with ℓ(⋅)=∥⋅∥\ell(\cdot)=\|\cdot\|. 5.3 Representation rate for a compressed output

Definition 11 (Bounded Distortion).

A distortion measure is said to be bounded if the maximum value of the distortion is ﬁnite:

dmax=max𝐯^∈𝒱d,𝐯∗∈𝒱d⁡d⁡(𝐯^,𝐯∗),d_{\mathrm{max}}=\max_{\hat{\mathbf{v}}\in\mathcal{V}^{d},\mathbf{v}^{*}\in\mathcal{V}^{d}}d(\hat{\mathbf{v}},\mathbf{v}^{*}), (20)

Where 𝐯^=𝐡Ψ​(𝐱)\hat{\mathbf{v}}=\mathbf{h}_{\Psi}(\mathbf{x}) is the model’s output, 𝐯∗\mathbf{v}^{*} is the ground truth, and d⁡(𝐱,𝐲)d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) is a distortion measure.

Theorem 12 (Embedding rate-distortion for a bijective mapping).

Assume a training set that is generated by randomly drawing samples from PXP_{X} and labeling them by the target function g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot), Ψ={{𝐱i,𝐯i}i=1m:𝐱i∼PX,𝐯i=g(𝐱i),𝐱i∈𝒳n×1,𝐯i∈𝒱d×1}\Psi=\big\{\{\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{v}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}:\mathbf{x}_{i}\sim P_{X},\quad\mathbf{v}_{i}=g(\mathbf{x}_{i}),\ \mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathcal{X}^{n\times 1},\ \mathbf{v}_{i}\in\mathcal{V}^{d\times 1}\big\}. g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot) is a deterministic bijective function. For nn and dd sufficiently large, the rate-distortion function of a source XX, and an output V^\hat{V} with distortion d⁡(v,v^)d(v,\hat{v})

ℛ(D)=minPV^|X:E⁡[d⁡(v,v^)]≤DI(X,V^)=H(X)−maxPV^|X:E⁡[d⁡(v,v^)]≤DH(X|V^)\mathcal{R}(D)=\min_{P_{\hat{V}|X}:E[d(v,\hat{v})]\leq D}I(X,\hat{V})=H(X)-\max_{P_{\hat{V}|X}:E[d(v,\hat{v})]\leq D}H(X|\hat{V}) (21)

is the minimum achievable rate. Therefore,

𝒬z≥n​I​(X,V^).\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{z}}\geq nI(X,\hat{V}). (22)

Note that in a specific setting where d⁡(⋅)=ℓ⁡(⋅)d(\cdot)=\ell(\cdot), the expected distortion E⁡[d⁡(v,v^)]=ℒ⁡(hΨ)E[d(v,\hat{v})]=\mathcal{L}(h_{\Psi}) is the generalization error.

In (Pereg, 2023a) we defined the terms for the sample complexity to yield a diminishing generalization error. Here we assumed that the training set is large enough.

We can now combine the two main results that we have proved so far.

5.4 Representation rate for noisy input and compressed output

Theorem 13 (Source-channel representation rate-distortion).

Let (X,V)∼PX,V(X,V)\sim P_{X,V} be an ergodic input-output probability mass function we will refer to as a source. A sequence of nn input symbols 𝐱∈𝒳n×1\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}^{n\times 1} is the input of a discrete channel PY|XP_{Y|X}. The output of the channel 𝐲∈𝒴n×1\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{Y}^{n\times 1} is mapped onto the reconstruction alphabet 𝐯^=hΨ​(𝐲)\hat{\mathbf{v}}=h_{\Psi}(\mathbf{y}), hΨ:𝒴n×1→𝒱d×1h_{\Psi}:\mathcal{Y}^{n\times 1}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}^{d\times 1}. Let D=E​d​(𝐯,𝐯^)D=Ed(\mathbf{v},\hat{\mathbf{v}}) be the average distortion achieved by this combined scheme. A source with rate-distortion ℛ⁡(D)\mathcal{R}(D) can be sent over a channel of capacity 𝒞\mathcal{C} and recovered with distortion DD if and only if ℛ⁡(D)<𝒞\mathcal{R}(D)<\mathcal{C}.

ℛ⁡(D)≤I⁡(X,V^)≤I⁡(X,Y)≤𝒞.\mathcal{R}(D)\leq I(X,\hat{V})\leq I(X;Y)\leq\mathcal{C}. (23)

Thus, the representation rate obeys,

I⁡(X,V^)<𝒬~zn<I⁡(X,Y).I(X,\hat{V})<\frac{\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}_{\mathrm{z}}}{n}<I(X;Y). (24)

Proof. See Appendix D.

6 Conclusions &\& Discussion

A core question in understanding learning mechanisms relies in understanding whether information about the input is fully preserved in the corresponding representation. In this study, we investigated desired properties of signal representation based on the expected rate of information “communicated” by the learning model. We attempt to formalize trade-offs and to answer the question: What is the capacity of a machine learning model to compute a desired function? (Viterbi, 2025). As intuitively expected, for a bijective mapping, the representation rate is directly determined by the entropy of the source. In a noisy environment, or when there are multiple possible observations of the source input, the maximal non-zero support of the embedding can only be up to the number of distinguishable signals determined by the mutual information between the source and the observed input. If the representation is compressed, the minimal representation rate for a given distortion, is determined by the mutual information between the source and the compressed output. We observed that the constraints on the representation-rate in different settings directly affect the required embedding cardinality and embedding dimensionality.

Recent work has established that language models are injectives and hence invertible. That is, decoder-only transformers almost surely map different prompts to different hidden states (Nikolaou et al., 2025). The authors postulate that collisions can never occur under gradient-based training. In other words, transformer representations are structurally lossless. More often than not, it is assumed that different inputs could collapse to the same hidden state, making exact recovery of the input impossible. That is, representations discard information that is critical for inversion of the task, which raises concerns for transparency, robustness, and safe deployment, as it suggests that the link between input and its representation is inherently lossy. Here we addressed related settings in a more general framework, revealing inherent limitations of representation learning. An interesting direction for future work could empirically investigate the proposed theory and its practical utility for LLMs.

In addition to the theoretical analysis above, our future work will continue to explore and analyze specific examples and applications as well as the practical implications of representation information-theoretic bounds, the resulting constraints on architecture’s choice, and possibilities for improvements in efficient learning. We noted that the established theorems are independent of the hypothesis class of hΨ​(⋅)h_{\Psi}(\cdot). That is, if the representation rate at the final layer of the encoder is insufficient at the representation level, no architecture can compensate for that. That said, the architecture leading to the final embedding layer and from the embedding to the target may affect the performance of the estimation. Our future work will further investigate these concerns.

Appendix B Proof of Theorem 8 - Representation Capacity

Proof.

We analyze a representation as shown in Figure 2. The proof follows the outline of achievability of Shannon channel coding theorem (Kramer and others, 2008). We assume paired ground truth signals {𝐱i,𝐯i}i=1M\{\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{v}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M}, M=2n​ℛM=2^{n\mathcal{R}}. Denote the original “message” ww, drawn from the index set {1,2,…,M}\{1,2,...,M\}, which results in the signal 𝐱w\mathbf{x}_{w} that goes through a system (aka channel) (noise, degradation, quantization…) and is received by the model (neural network) as a random sequence 𝐲∼PY|X(⋅|𝐱)\mathbf{y}\sim P_{Y|X}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}). The input to the learning model is 𝐲\mathbf{y}. The neural net’s encoder then yields the representation 𝐳=ℱ⁡(𝐲)\mathbf{z}=\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{y}). The decoder obtains the output 𝐯^\hat{\mathbf{v}} that corresponds with the pair {𝐱i,𝐯i}\{\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{v}_{i}\} with index i=w^i=\hat{w}. That is, 𝐯^=hΨ​(𝐲)=𝒢⁡(𝐳)\hat{\mathbf{v}}=h_{\Psi}(\mathbf{y})=\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{z}). The model makes an error if w^\hat{w} is not the same as the index ww that was “transmitted”, that is if 𝐯^≠𝐯\hat{\mathbf{v}}\neq\mathbf{v}. Cost constraint: we further impose a cost constraint over the average cost function E​s​(𝐱,𝐲)≤SmaxEs(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\leq S_{\mathrm{max}}.

Definition 14.

An (M,n)(M,n) code for the channel (X,PY|X​(𝐲|𝐱),Y)(X,P_{Y|X}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}),Y) and the model hΨ=(ℱ⁡(𝐲),𝒢⁡(𝐳))h_{\Psi}=(\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{y}),\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{z})) consists of the following:

  1. 1.

    An index set {1,2,…,M}\{1,2,...,M\}.

  2. 2.

    An encoding function Xn:{1,2,…,M}→𝒳nX^{n}:\{1,2,...,M\}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}^{n}, yielding codewords xn​(1),xn​(2),…,xn​(M)x^{n}(1),x^{n}(2),...,x^{n}(M). The set of codewords is called the codebook.

  3. 3.

    A decoding representation ℱ:𝒴n→𝒵q\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{Y}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}^{q} which is a deterministic rule that assigns a representation to each possible received vector.

  4. 4.

    A decoding map 𝒢:𝒵q→𝒱d\mathcal{G}:\mathcal{Z}^{q}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}^{d} which is a deterministic rule that assigns an output to each representation.

hΨh_{\Psi} is the concatenation of ℱ\mathcal{F}, and 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

Note that in our setting the learning model that maps yny^{n} to zqz^{q} and then maps zqz^{q} to vdv^{d} (encoder-decoder in machine learning literature) is corresponding with the decoder in information theory literature discussing channel capacity. The encoding function corresponds with any heuristic stage determining the original ground truth which corresponds with the noisy or distorted measurement that is the input to the neural net from a set of indexes of possible inputs. This stage can also correspond with any preprocessing stage applied to the signal, which yields the input to the neural net, such as: rescaling, normalization, clipping and quantization. The goal is to find the maximum rate ℛ\mathcal{R} for which Pr[w^≠w]Pr[\hat{w}\neq w] is arbitrarily close to zero and thus find the required 𝒬z\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{z}} for the representation.

Similarly to (Pereg, 2023a), in this case, we assume PY|X​(𝐲|𝐱)P_{Y|X}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}), e.g., y=u⁡(x)+ey=u(x)+e, such that each possible yy input induces a probability mass function over the possible xx’s. By assumption, the model efficiently learns the mapping hΨ:𝐲→𝐯h_{\Psi}:\mathbf{y}\rightarrow\mathbf{v}, and therefore the corresponding ground truth xx’s are distinguishable. In other words, the same yy is not associated with two different xx’s. Since we assumed a surjective mapping f:𝒴n→𝒳nf:\mathcal{Y}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}^{n}, for a distinguishable subset of input sequences, there exists only one xnx^{n} that could have caused a particular yny^{n} with high probability. We can therefore reconstruct the sequence at the output with a negligible probability of error, by mapping the observations into the proper “widely spaced” hidden sequences. We can define the conditional entropy H⁡(Y|X)H(Y|X) assuming they are ergodic and have a stationary coupling (Gray, 2009). Defining their mutual information I⁡(X,Y)=H⁡(Y)−H⁡(Y|X)I(X;Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X), their jointly typical set follows similar properties (Cover and Thomas, 2006). Define B={(xn,yn):(xn,yn)∈Aϵn(PX,Y),yn∈Aϵn(PY),xn∈Aϵn(PX)}B=\{(x^{n},y^{n}):(x^{n},y^{n})\in A^{n}_{\epsilon}(P_{X,Y}),y^{n}\in A^{n}_{\epsilon}(P_{Y}),x^{n}\in A^{n}_{\epsilon}(P_{X})\},and Aϵn​(PX,Y|xn)={yn:(xn,yn)∈Aϵn​(PX,Y)}A^{n}_{\epsilon}(P_{X,Y}|x^{n})=\{y^{n}:(x^{n},y^{n})\in A^{n}_{\epsilon}(P_{X,Y})\}. Observe that Aϵn​(PX,Y|xn)=∅A^{n}_{\epsilon}(P_{X,Y}|x^{n})=\emptyset if xn∉Aϵn​(PX)x^{n}\notin A^{n}_{\epsilon}(P_{X}) (Kramer and others, 2008). For nn sufficiently large and small ϵ\epsilon,

Pr⁡[Yn∈Aϵn​(PX,Y|xn)|Xn=xn]=1.\mathrm{Pr}[Y^{n}\in A^{n}_{\epsilon}(P_{X,Y}|x^{n})|X^{n}=x^{n}]=1. (27)
Pr[(xn,yn)∈B]=2−n​I​(X,Y).\mathrm{Pr}[(x^{n},y^{n})\in B]=2^{-nI(X;Y)}. (28)
|B|=2n​I​(X,Y).|B|=2^{nI(X;Y)}. (29)

Roughly speaking, if yny^{n} and xnx^{n} are jointly typical, then we can resolve an input yny^{n} as xnx^{n} and infer the correct vdv^{d}. There are approximately 2n​H​(Y|X)2^{nH(Y|X)} equally probable yny^{n} sequences, for each typical output sequence xnx^{n}. We assume that no two xnx^{n} sequences correspond to the same yny^{n} output sequence, otherwise, the learner will not be able to decide which xnx^{n} sequence it originated from. There are approximately 2n​H​(Y)2^{nH(Y)} possible typical yny^{n} sequences. This set is split into sets of size 2n​H​(Y|X)2^{nH(Y|X)}, associated with different xnx^{n} sequences. Therefore, the total number of distinguishable sets is less than or equal to 2n⁡(H⁡(Y)−H⁡(Y|X))=2n​I​(X,Y)2^{n(H(Y)-H(Y|X))}=2^{nI(X;Y)}. Hence, we can have at most 2n​I​(X,Y)2^{nI(X;Y)} disjoint sequences of length nn.

Appendix C Proof of the Theorem 12 - Representation rate-distortion

Proof.

We analyze a representation as shown in Figure 3. The proof follows the outline of achievability of rate-distortion region (Kramer and others, 2008). Rate distortion theory is concerned with quantization or lossy compression. Here we consider a different setting. A source PX​(⋅)P_{X}(\cdot) with alphabet 𝒳\mathcal{X} emits a sequence xnx^{n} that is passed to an encoder. The encoder ℱ:𝒳n→𝒵q\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{X}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}^{q} maps the input sequence to an embedding space of |𝒵|q=2n​ℛ|\mathcal{Z}|^{q}=2^{n\mathcal{R}} possible sequences zqz^{q}. The decoder 𝒢:𝒵q→𝒱^d\mathcal{G}:\mathcal{Z}^{q}\rightarrow\hat{\mathcal{V}}^{d} maps zqz^{q} into v^d\hat{v}^{d}. The goal is to ensure that the average non-negative and real-valued distortion is bounded E⁡[d⁡(vd,v^d)]≤DE[d(v^{d},\hat{v}^{d})]\leq D. We further assume that the maximum distortion is finite, i.e., d⁡(vd,v^d)≤dm​a​xd(v^{d},\hat{v}^{d})\leq d_{max}.

We define here the joint typical set, for nn and dd large enough,

Aϵn,d​(PX,V)=\displaystyle A^{n,d}_{\epsilon}(P_{X,V})= {(xn,vd)∈𝒳n×𝒱d:|−1nlog2PX,V(xn,vd)−H(X,V)|<ϵ\displaystyle\bigg\{(x^{n},v^{d})\in\mathcal{X}^{n}\times\mathcal{V}^{d}:\Big|-\frac{1}{n}\log_{2}P_{X,V}(x^{n},v^{d})-H(X,V)\Big|<\epsilon
xn∈𝒳n:|−1n​log2​PX​(xn)−H⁡(X)|<ϵ\displaystyle x^{n}\in\mathcal{X}^{n}:\Big|-\frac{1}{n}\log_{2}P_{X}(x^{n})-H(X)\Big|<\epsilon
vd∈𝒱d:|−1dlog2PV(vd)−H(V)|<ϵ}\displaystyle v^{d}\in\mathcal{V}^{d}:\Big|-\frac{1}{d}\log_{2}P_{V}(v^{d})-H(V)\Big|<\epsilon\bigg\} (35)

An achievable rate. Given xnx^{n}, output v^d\hat{v}^{d} such that (xn,v^d)∈Aϵn,d​(PX,V)(x^{n},\hat{v}^{d})\in A^{n,d}_{\epsilon}(P_{X,V}). To bound E​d​(vd,v^d)Ed(v^{d},\hat{v}^{d}) we partition the sample space into three events:

ℰ1={xn∉Aϵn(PX)},\mathcal{E}_{1}=\{x^{n}\notin A^{n}_{\epsilon}(P_{X})\}, (36)
ℰ2=ℰ1c⋂{⋂i=12n​ℛ{(xn,v^id)∉Aϵn,d(PX,V^)}},\mathcal{E}_{2}=\mathcal{E}^{c}_{1}\bigcap\Bigg\{\bigcap^{2^{n\mathcal{R}}}_{i=1}\big\{(x^{n},\hat{v}^{d}_{i})\notin A^{n,d}_{\epsilon}(P_{X,\hat{V}})\big\}\Bigg\}, (37)
ℰ3=(ℰ3∪ℰ3)c,\mathcal{E}_{3}=(\mathcal{E}_{3}\cup\mathcal{E}_{3})^{c}, (38)

where ℰ1c\mathcal{E}^{c}_{1} denotes the complement of ℰ1\mathcal{E}_{1}. Next, we apply the Theorem of Total Expectation,

E⁡[d⁡(vd,v^d)]=∑k=13P​r​[ℰk]​E​[d⁡(vd,v^d)|ℰk].E[d(v^{d},\hat{v}^{d})]=\sum^{3}_{k=1}Pr[\mathcal{E}_{k}]E[d(v^{d},\hat{v}^{d})|\mathcal{E}_{k}]. (39)
  1. 1.

    Suppose that xn​(w)∉Aϵn​(PX)x^{n}(w)\notin A^{n}_{\epsilon}(P_{X}), the upper bound on the average distortion is dmaxd_{\mathrm{max}}, but when nn is large Pr[xn(w)∉Aϵn(PX)]=0Pr[x^{n}(w)\notin A^{n}_{\epsilon}(P_{X})]=0.

Appendix D Proof of the Theorem 13 - Representation rate source-channel separation

Proof.

The proof follows similar outline to the proof of Source–Channel Separation Theorem
(El Gamal and Kim, 2011). We use a heuristic of separate lossy source coding and channel coding, although in practice in our setting there is no separation in the prediction stage.

Proof of achievability.

In Theorem 12 we have established that for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and for an input-output sequence {𝐱i,𝐯i}∼PX,V\{\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{v}_{i}\}\sim P_{X,V} there exists an estimator hΨh_{\Psi} that yields a lossy representations with rate ℛ⁡(D)\mathcal{R}(D) with an expected distortion less than or equal to DD. We treat the index ii for each sequence 𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i} as a message to be sent over the channel PY|XP_{Y|X}. By Theorem 8 the source sequence can be reliably mapped to 𝐯i\mathbf{v}_{i} from an input 𝐲i∼PY|X(⋅|𝐱)\mathbf{y}_{i}\sim P_{Y|X}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) if ℛ⁡(D)≤𝒞\mathcal{R}(D)\leq\mathcal{C}. The estimator predicts the reconstruction sequence corresponding with the received index. If the estimator makes an error, the distortion is upper bounded by dmaxd_{\mathrm{max}}. Because the probability of error tends to zero as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty, the overall expected distortion is less than or equal to DD.

Proof of the converse.

We wish to show that if a sequence of codes achieves the rate– distortion, then ℛ⁡(D)≤𝒞\mathcal{R}(D)\leq\mathcal{C}. By the converse proof of the lossy representation-distortion theorem, we know that

ℛ⁡(D)≤I⁡(X,V^).\mathcal{R}(D)\leq I(X,\hat{V}). (47)

Now, by the data processing inequality,

I⁡(X,V^)≤I⁡(X,Y).I(X,\hat{V})\leq I(X;Y). (48)

Following similar steps to the converse proof for embedding capacity, we therefore have

I⁡(X,V^)≤I⁡(X,Y)≤𝒞.I(X,\hat{V})\leq I(X;Y)\leq\mathcal{C}. (49)

Combining the above inequalities completes the proof of the converse. ∎

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.

We gratefully acknowledge support from our major funders, member institutions, , and all contributors.
